summary.name: Secure Shell (SSH)
summary.one_liner: SSH is a cryptographic network protocol for securely operating network services over an unsecured network, most notably remote login and command-line execution.
use_cases: logging into a remote server's command line
running a single command on a remote host
transferring files securely with SFTP or SCP
connecting to cloud virtual machines without exposing them directly
summary.what_it_does: The page describes SSH as a client-server protocol with three layers: transport (server authentication, encryption, integrity), user authentication (password, public key, keyboard-interactive, GSSAPI), and connection (multiplexing channels over one connection). It supports remote shells, command execution, port and X11 forwarding, and file transfer via SFTP, SCP, and rsync. Public-key authentication is described, including the ~/.ssh/authorized_keys file and the ssh-keygen utility. The page also covers the history from Tatu Ylönen's 1995 design through OpenSSH and the SSH-2 standard, plus known vulnerabilities and RFC standards.
notable: Designed by Tatu Ylönen in 1995 as a secure replacement for telnet, rsh and rlogin
OpenSSH is the most commonly implemented stack, released in 1999 by OpenBSD developers
SSH-1 is considered obsolete; SSH-2 became a standard in 2006
Includes an SSH3 alternative built on HTTP/3 and QUIC, and a 2026 Stanford-proposed Hop protocol
caveats: SSH-1 has design flaws and should be disabled in favor of SSH-2
The Terrapin attack (2023) requires both client and server to be upgraded; fixed in OpenSSH 9.6
Windows versions before 10 version 1709 do not include SSH by default
VPN functionality via SSH is only supported by OpenSSH server and client
